mFoco1: A hot spot is a 1 km square with fire on a given day. We divide the map into squares and flag the ones where a satellite picked up the heat of a fire: if the same square burns for three days, it counts three times.
mFocoKm: Today's satellites resolve detail down to 375 m, but we count in 1 km squares because that was the smallest unit the older satellites could see. With one unit for all of them, an early year can be compared with a recent one.
mFocoHora: Since 2012 the count comes from the S-NPP satellite, which passes over the peninsula twice a day: around {h} p.m. and again in the early hours of the morning. {n} in 100 hot spots come from the afternoon pass.
mFoco2: The satellite picks up any fire: it cannot tell a milpa burn from a wildfire. And no hot spots does not mean no fire, because clouds and smoke can hide it and a very small fire can slip through.
mUnirTitulo: How we joined 25 years of satellites
mUnir1: More satellites joined over the years, and adding up everything they all see would inflate recent years. So we use one satellite per period:
mUnir2: Today's VIIRS sensors detect smaller fires than the older MODIS ones: in the burning season, for every square where Aqua saw fire in Yucatán, S-NPP sees between {a} and {b}, depending on the zone. Using the years both satellites flew, we computed a factor for each zone and time of year and used it to bring the MODIS years to today's scale.
mPasoTitulo: Why not keep using Terra and Aqua?
mPasoLeyenda: Time each satellite passes over Yucatán, by year (median of its daytime hot spots).
mPaso1: Until {u}, Terra passed over Yucatán around {t0} a.m. and Aqua around {a0} p.m. Since then their orbits have been drifting: in {y}, Terra passes at {t1} a.m. and Aqua at {a1} p.m.
mPaso2: Because fire changes over the course of the day, a satellite whose overpass time shifts can no longer be compared with itself. That is why we do not use Terra or Aqua for recent years, even though both are still flying.
mPasoAria: Overpass time by year. Terra, around {t0} until {u} and {t1} in {y}. Aqua, around {a0} until {u} and {a1} in {y}. S-NPP, at almost the same time every year.
mFuera1: In {m}, {p} detections ({f} of {d}) come from a single spot that NASA's own system flags as a static heat source. It is not vegetation fire, so we do not count it.
mFuera2: Over the {n} years of the series, the satellite sent no data on {d} days; {r} of them were filled in with another satellite that passed the same day.

mConfiarIntro: We put four questions to the series. Each target was set before we saw the result.
mDetSalto2012: The target was to remove at least half of the jump and land between {m0} and {m1}. Between S-NPP periods, with no satellite change, the ratio ranges from {naturalMin} to {naturalMax}: that is normal year-to-year variation. For the state of Yucatán alone, the same calculation gives {razonCrudaYucatan} uncorrected and {razonArmonizadaYucatan} after correction.
mDetAqua: With a single factor for the whole peninsula, the error was {wapeUnicoPct}%; with one per zone and season, {wapeZonaEpocaPct}%. That is roughly how far off the years the series takes from Aqua may be.
mDetConafor: These are {incendios} wildfires recorded from {desde} to {hasta}. The target was at least three times as many fires with hot spots nearby as chance would give, and {meta} in 100 of the large ones.
mDetConaforDuracion: Longer fires are easier to catch: counting any satellite, not just S-NPP, {d1} in 100 one-day fires had hot spots nearby, against {d4} in 100 of those that lasted more than a week.

mSatTitulo: Compare each satellite with the series
mSatIntro: Pick a satellite and compare it with the series we use, one satellite per period (Yucatán, March 1 to May 31). Uncorrected, the MODIS satellites see far less fire than the VIIRS ones; once corrected, each should land close to the series.
mSatLeyFactor: Years used to compute its factor

mSatLecturaMismos: We measured this over {a}–{b}, the same years used to compute its factor, so it is not an independent check.

mSatNotaTerra: Terra is the oldest of the satellites, and NASA confirms it is drifting from its orbit; in recent years it falls below the series. The series only uses Terra until July 3, 2002.
mSatNotaAqua: Aqua carries the series from 2003 to 2011. In 2022 it went 17 days without sending data because of a fault NASA reported, and for the rest of that season it saw fewer hot spots than S-NPP. We do not know why yet.
mSatNotaSNPP: S-NPP is the reference: from January 20, 2012 to November 2, 2026 the series is S-NPP. The other satellites are brought to its scale.
mSatNotaNOAA20: NOAA-20 carries the series from November 3, 2026. Its FIRMS record starts on April 1, 2018, so it misses March that year.

mDescarga1: The complete harmonized series: every week from 2001 to 2026 in {n} municipalities of the peninsula, with the normal for each week. Our boundaries do not yet include the three newest municipalities (Dzitbalché, Seybaplaya and Puerto Morelos), so their fire is counted in the municipality they split from. It is a CSV file that opens in Excel, with a header row.

valSalto2012PasaDentro: Yes. For the whole peninsula over the full year, fire in {despuesDesde}–{despuesHasta} is {razonCruda} times the {antesDesde}–{antesHasta} level uncorrected and {razonArmonizada} times after correction (1 = no jump), within normal year-to-year variation.
valSalto2012PasaFuera: Partly. For the whole peninsula over the full year, fire in {despuesDesde}–{despuesHasta} is {razonCruda} times the {antesDesde}–{antesHasta} level uncorrected and {razonArmonizada} times after correction (1 = no jump): that meets the target but falls outside normal year-to-year variation, so part of the jump may still come from the satellite.
valSalto2012NoPasaDentro: No. For the whole peninsula over the full year, the correction removes {reduccionPct}% of the jump and leaves fire in {despuesDesde}–{despuesHasta} at {razonArmonizada} times the {antesDesde}–{antesHasta} level (1 = no jump): that misses the target, even though it is within normal year-to-year variation.
valSalto2012NoPasaFuera: No. For the whole peninsula over the full year, the correction removes {reduccionPct}% of the jump and leaves fire in {despuesDesde}–{despuesHasta} at {razonArmonizada} times the {antesDesde}–{antesHasta} level (1 = no jump): that misses the target, so years before 2012 cannot yet be compared with later ones.
valSalto2012Limitaciones: We only checked the 2012 satellite change, using three-year averages, not each year from 2001 to 2011.
Normal variation comes from comparing S-NPP periods between 2013 and 2025. There are seven and they overlap, so it is a reference point, not a statistical test.
We measured the whole peninsula over the full year. For a single municipality or a single season, the jump may differ.
valAquaFueraMuestraNombre: Does it hold up in held-out years?
valAquaFueraMuestraPasaZonaEpoca: Yes. In {desde}–{hasta}, years held out of the calibration, Aqua corrected by zone and season was off from S-NPP by {wapeZonaEpocaPct}% on average, under the 25% limit.
valAquaFueraMuestraPasaUnico: Yes, with a single factor. In {desde}–{hasta}, years held out of the calibration, Aqua with one factor was off from S-NPP by {wapeUnicoPct}% on average, under the 25% limit; splitting by zone and season does not improve on it enough ({wapeZonaEpocaPct}%).
valAquaFueraMuestraNoPasaZonaEpoca: No. In {desde}–{hasta}, years held out of the calibration, Aqua corrected by zone and season was off from S-NPP by {wapeZonaEpocaPct}% on average, over the 25% limit: the Aqua years, 2002 to 2011, may be further off than we accept.
valAquaFueraMuestraNoPasaUnico: No. In {desde}–{hasta}, years held out of the calibration, Aqua with one factor was off from S-NPP by {wapeUnicoPct}% on average, over the 25% limit: the Aqua years, 2002 to 2011, may be further off than we accept.
valAquaFueraMuestraLimitaciones: We compare against S-NPP, which does not see every fire either: this shows whether the satellites agree with each other, not how much fire there was.
The error pools five years and every zone; the chart breaks it down by year. For a single municipality or week it can be larger.

In 2022 Aqua went 17 days without sending data because of a fault NASA reported; we left those days out. For the rest of that season it saw fewer hot spots than usual relative to S-NPP, while Terra, its twin, did not. We do not know why yet.
We only tested Aqua. Terra, which covers 2001 to mid-2002, has no equivalent test.
valConaforNombre: Does it catch the wildfires CONAFOR recorded?
valConaforCumple: Yes. S-NPP had hot spots near {grandesSnpp} in 100 large wildfires (over 100 hectares) and near {realSnpp} in 100 of all of them, where {azarSnpp} would be expected by chance.
valConaforNoCumple: No. S-NPP had hot spots near {grandesSnpp} in 100 large wildfires (over 100 hectares) and near {realSnpp} in 100 of all of them, where {azarSnpp} would be expected by chance: that misses the target.
valConaforLimitaciones: This question only checks whether the satellite detects wildfires; it says nothing about how years are carried from one satellite to another.
CONAFOR's records are wildfires from 2015 to 2024, not agricultural burns, so this says nothing about burn dates.
We count any hot spot within 2 km, from one day before to one day after the fire. Since there is fire everywhere during the season, we also measured how much would match by chance.
Small fires are missed more often: of those of 5 hectares or less, {chicosSnpp}% had hot spots nearby.
valViirsNombre: Can NOAA-20 carry the series on?
valViirsNumero: NOAA-20: {razonMinNoaa20} to {razonMaxNoaa20} per S-NPP hot spot
valViirsPasaNoaa21Cumple: Yes. From {aniosDesde} to {aniosHasta}, NOAA-20 with its factor counted between {razonMinNoaa20} and {razonMaxNoaa20} hot spots per S-NPP hot spot, inside the 0.90–1.10 target every year, so the series can continue without a jump like 2012's. NOAA-21 also stays within the target in its two full years ({razonMinNoaa21} to {razonMaxNoaa21}).
valViirsPasaNoaa21NoCumple: Yes. From {aniosDesde} to {aniosHasta}, NOAA-20 with its factor counted between {razonMinNoaa20} and {razonMaxNoaa20} hot spots per S-NPP hot spot, inside the 0.90–1.10 target every year, so the series can continue without a jump like 2012's. NOAA-21 misses the target in its two full years ({razonMinNoaa21} to {razonMaxNoaa21}), so it is not part of the series.
valViirsNoPasaNoaa21Cumple: No. From {aniosDesde} to {aniosHasta}, NOAA-20 with its factor counted between {razonMinNoaa20} and {razonMaxNoaa20} hot spots per S-NPP hot spot, with a total difference of {diferenciaPctNoaa20}%; the target was 0.90–1.10 every year and at most 5% overall, so switching to NOAA-20 could put a jump in the series. NOAA-21 does stay within the target in its two full years ({razonMinNoaa21} to {razonMaxNoaa21}).
valViirsNoPasaNoaa21NoCumple: No. From {aniosDesde} to {aniosHasta}, NOAA-20 with its factor counted between {razonMinNoaa20} and {razonMaxNoaa20} hot spots per S-NPP hot spot, with a total difference of {diferenciaPctNoaa20}%; the target was 0.90–1.10 every year and at most 5% overall, so switching to NOAA-20 could put a jump in the series. NOAA-21 misses it too in its two full years ({razonMinNoaa21} to {razonMaxNoaa21}).
valViirsLimitaciones: We computed NOAA-20's factor from these same years, so the factor pulls the total difference ({diferenciaPctNoaa20}%) toward zero. What tells you something is each year on its own.
We compare VIIRS satellites with each other: this shows whether the series jumps when the satellite changes, not whether they see every fire.
NOAA-21 has been in FIRMS since March 2023, so it overlaps S-NPP for only two full years. It has no factor and is not part of the series.
